sections.title: The commission, a second time
sections.line: A reluctant prophet and the shortest sermon in scripture.

sections.title: Nineveh believes, top to bottom
sections.line: King, people and livestock in sackcloth, hoping God might relent.

sections.title: God relents, Jonah rages
sections.line: The mercy Jonah dreaded arrives, and he asks to die.

sections.title: Argued out of his own pity
sections.line: God turns Jonah's grief for a plant into a question.

themes.note: Three times the word turns: God may, God did, God does.
God's fierce anger cools; Jonah's never does.
A vine, a worm, a wind — three appointments, one lesson.
Called great at the start and at the end, never by Jonah.

references.why: Jonah recites Israel's own creed about mercy — and recites it as a complaint, which is the joke of the book.
The potter passage states the rule this narrative enacts: a threatened disaster is revocable if the nation turns.
Supplies the 'who knows?' of hopeful repentance — David's words over a dying child, now in pagan mouths.
Elijah under the broom tree asking to die, so Jonah's sulk reads as a prophet's posture God has indulged before.
Jesus turns Nineveh's repentance into an accusation against his own generation: the pagans managed it.

purpose.statement: The author wants us to know God relents when a people turn, because the threat in a prophet's mouth was always an invitation rather than a verdict.
He wants us to watch Jonah grieve a dead plant more than a living city, so that we notice how small our own pity has become.
He wants us to believe that mercy reaches past Israel to 120,000 strangers and their cattle, because the book ends on that question and never answers it.
